diagnosis.what_is_wrong: No kernel evidence establishes a host or service fault causing the coding task to run longer than usual. The trace shows changing workloads, including python3 using about 0.24–0.25 CPU-seconds per second in the late active phase, but this is not host-wide CPU saturation on a machine with at least four CPUs, and the trace provides no latency baseline or demonstrated scheduling delay.
diagnosis.evidence: Compared the full 03:17:26.200–03:17:59.000 trace using the workers’ full-span event counts and per-second scheduler/CPU summaries. Scheduler and several other event rates declined around 03:17:31, with only a brief pulse at 03:17:33, while measured CPU fell from about 253 ms/s in 03:17:26.2–31.2 to 83 ms/s in 03:17:31.2–41.2, then returned to about 254 ms/s in 03:17:41.2–54.2 as the workload shifted from claude/JITWorker to python3. In the late phase python3 accounted for about 2.956 CPU-seconds over 13 seconds; raw sched_switch records show it selected on CPU 3, while other CPUs show idle activity. Checked competing mechanisms: 556 block requests issued and 558 completed, sampled network transmissions returned rc=0, no coherent container restart was found, and inspected wakeups do not demonstrate a long wake-to-run delay. These checks do not prove the task met its expected duration, but they do not support a kernel-level fault diagnosis.
diagnosis.window_evidence: The 32.8-second trace begins at 03:17:26.200 and ends at 03:17:59.000. The major measured changes are a workload/rate decline around 03:17:31 and a CPU/workload recovery around 03:17:41, but there is no evidence these delimit a fault rather than ordinary task/workload transitions. The trace starts during the initially high activity and has no pre-trace baseline, so no incident start or duration is defensible.
